text: What does a bullet through the liver do to me?

args.label: Gunshot wound to the liver
args.source: Own estimate of moderate haemorrhage (ATLS class II–III shock pattern); not from published model data

feelings.label: Pain
feelings.cause: Torn liver capsule and abdominal lining irritated by blood

stops.label: Wound
stops.say: The bullet tears liver tissue packed with blood vessels; blood pours into the belly.

stops.label: Heart races
stops.say: With less blood returning, the heart beats faster and vessels squeeze to hold pressure.

stops.label: Saving blood
stops.say: Blood is diverted from kidneys and gut to keep brain and heart supplied.

stops.label: Faintness
stops.say: If bleeding continues, less blood reaches the brain: dizziness, confusion.

steps.title: The wound
steps.say: A shot from the front crosses the liver and, in the model, the base of the right lung. The liver is full of blood, so torn tissue bleeds into the belly.

composed.caption: Bullet track through liver tissue
composed.basis: Textbook trauma surgery: liver injuries bleed from low-pressure veins and the capsule; illustration only

steps.title: The lung too
steps.say: A path that grazes the lung base can let air or blood into the chest, so breathing gets harder and faster. Any wound there makes it more urgent.

steps.title: The heart compensates
steps.say: Less blood comes back to the heart, so it speeds up and vessels tighten. In this estimate, your pulse climbs from about 78 to 113 within half an hour.

steps.title: Saving the brain
steps.say: Pressure still falls, from about 119 to 95. Blood is pulled from gut and kidneys to keep brain and heart going, so you may feel cold, pale and faint.

steps.title: The clock
steps.say: Within the hour this model has you down well over a litre of fluid. Compensation buys time but can't plug the hole, and when it gives out, pressure collapses.

steps.title: What saves you
steps.say: Pressure on the wound, a fast trip to a trauma centre, blood transfusion, and surgery to pack or stitch the liver. Many liver wounds survive with quick care.

composed.caption: Surgery packs and seals the tear
composed.basis: Damage-control surgery and perihepatic packing, standard trauma practice; illustration only

lines.text: The main danger is bleeding: the liver is full of blood, and it pours into the belly.
In my estimate your pulse climbs to about 113 and pressure falls, buying maybe an hour.
What saves people is fast trauma surgery and transfusion, and many survive with quick care.
